mathematical_justification: All 16 parents were read. Ideal-power quotients, prime quotients, polynomial-presentation quotients, square-zero quotients, and S_q/pS_q share the additive-coset construction with induced multiplication. Well-definedness follows because changing representatives by elements of an ideal changes sums/products by elements of that ideal. This is not an additive/module quotient alone: Z/2 as an additive quotient carries no general recipe for multiplying arbitrary quotient modules; the ring construction needs multiplication on the parent and an ideal. Quotients can be nonfields (Z/4), so the existing special field k[t]/(f) for irreducible f cannot resolve this general identity. Localization inverts a multiplicative set instead of killing an ideal. However occ.39767a08c003da7e344c in formally-smooth-ring-map has a compound context: an R-algebra, square-zero ideal, quotient algebra AND canonical quotient map, described as an extension. The underlying ring quotient is a justified shared prerequisite, but a whole square-zero extension datum is not identical to a quotient-ring object. Existing aliasing is not certified as equality of those compound objects by this review.

descriptor.context: Kernel or null space of a linear map between vector spaces over a common field

form.wave2.cross107.field-vector-linear-.context: Kernel or null space of a linear map between vector spaces over a common field
form.wave2.cross107.field-vector-linear-.text: For vector spaces V,W over a common field K and a K-linear transformation T:V→W, its kernel (null space) is ker T={v∈V:T(v)=0_W}=T⁻¹({0_W}), the preimage of the zero vector in W.

descriptor.context: Kernel of a linear map between left R-modules

form.wave2.cross107.module-linear-kernel.context: Kernel of a linear map between left R-modules
form.wave2.cross107.module-linear-kernel.text: Let φ:M→N be an R-linear map between left R-modules over the same associative ring R. The kernel is ker φ=φ⁻¹({0_N})={m∈M:φ(m)=0_N}, where 0_N is the identity of the additive group of N.

descriptor.context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping

form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.1.context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping
form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.1.text: For a total map f:S→T, the image im(f) is {t∈T:there exists s∈S with f(s)=t}, the set of values actually attained by f.

form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.2.context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping
form.wave2.cross110.image-of-mapping.2.text: Equivalently, for a total map f:S→T the image is f[S]={f(s):s∈S}, the direct image of the entire domain S.

descriptor.context: Foundational mapping as total single-valued assignment X→Y

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-element-as.context: Foundational mapping as total single-valued assignment X→Y
form.wave2.foundation.mapping-element-as.text: Given sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y assigns to every x∈X exactly one value f(x)∈Y. Equivalently, for each x∈X there exists a unique y∈Y that the assignment associates with x.

descriptor.context: Set-theoretic mapping as typed graph (X,Y,G)

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-typed-grap.text: For sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y can be defined as a typed relation (X,Y,G) where G⊆X×Y and, for every x∈X, there exists exactly one y∈Y with (x,y)∈G. The graph is G; X and Y are part of the mapping data.

mathematical_justification: All 14 parents were read. Formal polynomial algebras occur with one, finite, or arbitrary set-indexed variables, including S-indexed variables in the naive cotangent complex. Finite support of each polynomial does not force the whole variable family to be finite; a finite-variable specialization is not a reason to restrict the generic missing algebra to finite rank. A polynomial ring is not a degree predicate, a quotient by equations, or an evaluated element. In particular occ.aa7d5dd9a4e322c869e6 (strongly-transcendental-subring-element) has context explicitly allowing an indeterminate OR its evaluation at x∈S. Evaluation can lose information: T and 0 in R[T] have the same value at x=0 but are different formal polynomials. A polynomial-algebra prerequisite is justified for coefficient expressions, but the current mixed context must not be treated as a proof that a polynomial and its value, or a ring and one element, are the identical object. The nonzero-polynomial qualifier in the algebraic-extension source remains a source restriction, not an exclusion of zero from the polynomial algebra itself.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The residue field of a commutative local ring (R,m) is precisely R/m. That R/m is a field follows from maximality of m; it is not an arbitrary quotient ring and no prime localization is presumed when m is already maximal. mathematical_justification: All 11 parents were read: local/Tor/regularity criteria, fibre constructions, Henselian lifting, fibrewise maps, relative assassin, syntomic fibres and coefficient rings. They use A/m for the specified commutative local ring, including A=R_p and scheme local rings. For a proper maximal ideal m in a unital commutative A, a∉m gives (a)+m=A, so ra+b=1 for some b∈m; [r] inverts [a]. Thus A/m is a field, but a bare field definition does not specify its quotient construction, map or relation to (A,m). Generic quotient rings need not be fields, and Frac(D) preserves an embedded domain instead of killing a maximal ideal. For A=Z_(p), its residue field has characteristic p while Frac(A)=Q has characteristic zero, disproving a general residue/fraction-field identification. In coefficient-ring contexts an induced residue-field isomorphism is a map between such fields, not the residue field itself.

form.f0d993a60533fc99.groupoid-valued-pr.text: A (strict) groupoid-valued presheaf on a category C is a functor F:C^op→Groupoids, assigning a groupoid F(U) to every object U and a pullback functor f*:F(U)→F(V) to each arrow f:V→U. Pullbacks preserve identities and compose strictly: (f∘g)*=g*∘f*.

form.f7206eb9332b9389.category-valued-pr.text: A (strict) category-valued presheaf on a category C is a functor F:C^op→Cat (equivalently, a contravariant functor from C to Cat). It assigns a category F(U) to each object U and a pullback functor f*:F(U)→F(V) to every arrow f:V→U, with (f∘g)*=g*∘f* and (id_U)* the identity functor.

form.wave2.foundation.category-functor.text: A covariant functor F:A→B between small categories assigns to every object x of A an object F(x) of B and to every arrow f:x→y an arrow F(f):F(x)→F(y). For composable arrows f,g it satisfies F(g∘f)=F(g)∘F(f), and F(id_x)=id_{F(x)}.

form.wave2.foundation.pseudofunctor-to-s.text: A pseudofunctor P:A→C from an ordinary category A to a strict 2-category C assigns objects P(x) and 1-morphisms P(f), invertible comparison 2-cells η_x:id_{P(x)}⇒P(id_x) and κ_{g,f}:P(g∘f)⇒P(g)∘P(f), and satisfies the unit identities κ_{id_y,f}=η_y⋆id_{P(f)}, κ_{f,id_x}=id_{P(f)}⋆η_x and the associativity coherence (id_{P(h)}⋆κ_{g,f})∘κ_{h,g∘f}=(κ_{h,g}⋆id_{P(f)})∘κ_{h∘g,f} for composable f,g,h.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The diagram F:I→C in the limit and colimit sources is the same covariant functor between an index category and an ambient category, with no assumed smallness of both categories. Cone versus cocone direction is not encoded in this prerequisite.

Both flatness and faithful flatness sources involve precisely the covariant tensoring functor N↦N⊗_R M on R-modules and its action on morphisms. Faithfulness/reflection of exactness adds a distinct defining condition but does not change the tensor functor.

The connected-limit/colimit source references a diagram with a connected indexing category; the ordinary diagram prerequisite is the functor D:I→C. Its context explicitly takes I small, a source-specific indexing restriction. It does not impose smallness on arbitrary C or identify connected diagrams with general diagrams as parent notions.

Finite limit/colimit sources invoke a diagram F:I→C where the index category has finitely many objects and morphisms. This is the general diagram-as-functor construction, specialized to finite and hence small indexing I; the finite index restriction and target locally-small convention remain source-specific.

The covariant representability source invokes F:C→Sets, an ordinary covariant functor into the category of sets, which is an instance of the generic functor F:C→D. Its set-valuedness and any local-smallness convention remain parent-specific; generic functorial identity/composition laws are the shared prerequisite.

The category-fibred-in-sets source invokes the ordinary covariant functor p:E→C from total category to base category without assumed smallness. This is the same general identity/composition-preserving category functor prerequisite as the unrestricted F:C→D used in 2-categories and fibrations; p is merely a variable name. The cartesian-lift and discrete-fibre conditions remain parent-specific and are not imposed on all functors.

The limit/colimit and finite-diagram sources define a diagram F:I→C as an ordinary identity/composition-preserving functor from an indexing category I to an arbitrary target category C, not a small-to-small functor. Thus a diagram's underlying functor is precisely the unrestricted ordinary-functor prerequisite; index finiteness, connectedness, cone structure and universal limit/colimit claims remain parent-specific.

The iso-comma-category source requires two ordinary covariant functors F:A→C and G:B→C, each preserving identities and composition without any smallness restriction. This invokes the general unrestricted ordinary-functor prerequisite twice; their shared codomain, the objects (a,b,α) and the iso-comma compatibility equations remain conditions only of the parent iso-comma construction.

The left-adjoint source uses ordinary functors L:C→D and R:D→C, differing only in domain/codomain orientation and naming from a generic identity/composition-preserving functor. Adjointness, naturality of Hom-bijections, and the fact that L and R have opposite domain assignments are extra parent constraints, not properties of an arbitrary functor.

The two-category-of-fibred-sets source uses functors H:E→E′ of total categories, ordinary functors at the level of objects/arrows, with the additional equation p′H=p. The general unrestricted functor prerequisite is identical while the over-base compatibility and fibration hypotheses remain source-specific and do not follow from ordinary functoriality.

A tensor bifunctor ⊗:C×C→C in a monoidal category is an ordinary covariant functor with source the product category C×C, preserving identities and compositions for pairs of arrows. Its bifunctor notation does not introduce a different functoriality axiom. Product-category construction, tensor object, associator and monoidal coherence remain source-specific and are not collapsed into arbitrary functor meaning.

In flat and faithfully flat module definitions, the operation N↦N⊗_R M, with morphism action f↦f⊗id_M, is a covariant functor between the categories of R-modules, preserving identities and composition and with no small-category hypothesis. This uses the same generic functor prerequisite; the tensor-product implementation and (reflection and) preservation of exactness are additional parent-specific requirements.

The projective-module Hom exactness source's covariant Hom_R(P,−) takes an R-module N to Hom_R(P,N) and a morphism g to postcomposition g∘−, preserving identities and compositions. Thus it is a typed instance of unrestricted ordinary functoriality. The choice of Hom construction, additivity, and exactness condition remain attached to the projectivity source, and no restriction to small categories is imported.

mathematical_justification: All 36 parents were read. Ordinary diagrams, projections and over-base functors, tensor bifunctors on product categories, exact functors, adjoint pairs, localizations and Hom/tensor functors all use ordinary covariant functor data in their correctly typed domains. A diagram I→C with small/finite I does not make C small, so it is not covered by the existing small-to-small functor definition. An inverse system is covariant on I^op; a represented presheaf is covariant C^op→Sets. In category/groupoid-valued presheaves the current source explicitly uses C^op→Cat/Groupoids with strict composition, not another contravariance on C^op. Opposite directions of the two functors in an adjunction do not make either contravariant. Tensoring maps sends g to g⊗id, and Hom_R(P,−) sends g to postcomposition, both covariantly; these actions are not merely tensor/Hom objects. Extra exactness, monoidal structure, over-base equations and pseudofunctor comparison cells remain separate. The generic strict-functor prerequisite is missing under the checked inventory; no alias to a contravariant or smallness-constrained meaning is justified.

mathematical_justification: All 11 parents were read. Five explicitly require an identity: commutative prime/maximal ideals, field, integral domain, and Noetherian module over a commutative ring with identity. Their additional properness, nonzeroness, invertibility or Noetherianity belongs to the parent, not to the bare ring candidate. mathematical_justification: All 11 parents were read. Finite free R^n in presentations and Lazard diagrams, arbitrary R^(I) in resolutions/direct-summand characterizations, and free modules over localized rings instantiate the same basis/direct-sum construction while preserving rank and coefficient-ring restrictions in the parent. Finite support of each vector in a direct sum does not imply the index set is finite: over a nonzero field the infinitely many standard basis vectors cannot be spanned by a finite list, whose union of supports is finite. Existing finitely generated modules need not be free (Z/2 as a Z-module has torsion), and locally free/projective modules need not be globally free: for R=k×k, eR with e=(1,0) is a finite direct summand of R and locally free with component ranks (1,0), whereas any globally free R^n has ranks (n,n). The already-adjudicated free-resolution augmentation forces its terminal module to be unital under its recorded free-module construction. No rank-finiteness, projectivity-only, or local-free meaning can resolve the missing general free module.

A quotient set forgets both addition and scalar action, and the quotient-group meaning supplies no R-action. A generic quotient module has no required multiplication: for example the Z-module Z/2⊕Z/3 has no multiplication specified by its module data. mathematical_justification: The eight occurrences test f(x)=f(y)⇒x=y for specified maps: evaluation, field-tensor multiplication, scalar multiplication, tensor comparisons and fibre maps. For additive maps this is equivalent to zero kernel, since f(x)=f(y) iff f(x−y)=0, but the module-kernel construction is not the general predicate. Ordinary injectivity is weaker than universal tensor injectivity: multiplication by 2 on Z is injective, while tensoring with Z/2 yields the zero map on Z/2. Thus the existing pure-monomorphism meaning is not a resolution. A map can be injective without surjectivity (inclusion {0}→{0,1}); no bijection, inverse function or categorical isomorphism follows. Field embeddings retain their ring axioms separately, and no default algebraic independence is inferred without the appropriate quantified evaluation map. No checked mapping definition supplies the missing predicate.

mathematical_justification: Each of the seven contexts requires an arrow with a two-sided inverse in its stated category: locally ringed spaces, topological groups, commutative rings, a localization, a small groupoid, or an abelian category. If g and h are both inverses, g=g(fh)=(gf)h=h, so the inverse is unique, but all structure in the ambient morphisms must remain. A bijective continuous map need not be a homeomorphism: the identity from a discrete two-point space to its indiscrete topology has no continuous inverse. Consequently a set bijection, a plain homeomorphism without group/sheaf data, and an isomorphism of graphs cannot resolve generic categorical invertibility. In the abelian-category sentence the phrase isomorphism of categorical morphisms means the comparison arrow Coim(f)→Im(f) is invertible, not an isomorphism between arrows in an arrow category. Specialized aliases are justified only as instances of this predicate with ambient category retained.

form.wave2.real45.dedekind-supremum.text: An ordered set (S,≤) has the Dedekind completeness property if every nonempty subset A⊆S that has an upper bound in S possesses a least upper bound sup(A)∈S. existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The ordered-set Dedekind completeness and complete-ordered-real-field sources invoke the same least-upper-bound notion: an upper bound of a subset A no larger than any other upper bound. The order/field axioms remain separately required.

The bounded-operator norm source takes sup of the set {||Tx||:||x||≤1}; the Dedekind completeness source defines least upper bound sup(A) in an ordered set. The operator-norm supremum is a special bounded nonempty real-set instance, not a distinct supremum predicate.

Depth source takes the supremum of nonnegative lengths of M-regular sequences contained in an ideal. The underlying order operation is the least upper bound of the set of lengths in the ordered set ℕ∪{∞}, precisely the general poset-supremum construction. The extended value ∞, restriction to M-regular sequences, and containment in I remain defining source-context qualifications.

The finite-module-dimension source takes suprema of lengths of prime chains in Supp_R(M). These are least upper bounds in ℕ∪{∞} just as for any subset of an ordered set, with +∞ for unbounded integer lengths. The prime-chain restriction and support of M are parent-specific and do not become part of the abstract supremum prerequisite.

The scheme-size source takes a least upper bound of a set of cardinal numbers ordered by cardinal comparison. This shares only the abstract poset supremum construction sup(A) as least upper bound with other ordered-set sources. The ambient order here is the cardinal order (not the ordered reals), the values are cardinals and the result is a cardinal supremum, all retained as source-specific typing; no cardinal/real-value identification is asserted.

mathematical_justification: In all six parents the common operation is least upper bound in a specified order, not its existence for every subset. If u and v both satisfy the upper-bound/least conditions then u≤v and v≤u, so antisymmetry gives u=v. The existing Dedekind completeness meaning is a quantified existence property of an ordered set, not the supremum of an individual subset. In the real-field and operator-norm sources, nonempty bounded real sets are used (the norm ball contains zero and boundedness gives a finite bound); cardinal supremum is taken in cardinal order, not real order. Depth and module dimension use extended nonnegative integers, with infinity for unbounded length sets. A supremum need not be attained: (0,1) in R has supremum 1 without a maximum. Thus maximum, completeness and metric completion are not generic resolutions. The depth convention IM=M⇒∞ is separately stipulated, not derived as a finite maximum.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: A polynomial f∈R[T] is monic when its leading coefficient is the unit 1_R, precisely the same defining property of a monic polynomial over a field k. Simple-root lifting and the residue field remain different independent prerequisites.

Both source contexts use the standard leading-coefficient-equals-one predicate for a polynomial over a commutative unital coefficient ring. The étale polynomial's quotient and the minimal polynomial's irreducibility are additional constraints, not part of this shared prerequisite. Compared the entire source for 'monic polynomial f' against canonical candidate 'monic polynomial'; source phrasing remains immutable.

The integrality-of-element and integral-ring-map formulations both require a monic polynomial whose coefficients originate in R and whose evaluation in S vanishes. Saying 'coefficients in the image of R' is equivalent to evaluating a monic R[T]-polynomial under R→S; injectivity of R→S is not assumed.

Integral-element and integral-ring-map formulations use a monic polynomial to test vanishing at an element; standard étale maps and minimal polynomials also use the leading-coefficient-one predicate. The common prerequisite is being monic; satisfaction of a monic equation or étaleness is not identified.

An element integral over an ideal is tested by a positive-degree monic polynomial P(T), and étale/minimal-polynomial definitions use a univariate polynomial with leading coefficient 1. The monic predicate is shared; positive degree and coefficient conditions a_j∈I^{d-j} stay parent-specific.

mathematical_justification: All six sources require leading coefficient 1 in the commutative univariate polynomial algebra. Monicity does not imply irreducibility: T² is monic and reducible over a field; 2T+1 over Q is degree one and irreducible but not monic as written. Degree is a number attached to a nonzero polynomial, while monicity constrains a coefficient. A minimal polynomial additionally generates an evaluation kernel; étale presentation and Henselian lifting add derivative or root conditions; ideal integrality imposes d≥1 and prescribed ideal-power coefficients. For a unital coefficient map with nonzero target, a monic polynomial keeps its leading coefficient after mapping, and finitely many image coefficients may be lifted to coefficients in R; no injectivity of R→S is needed. The generic monic candidate includes constant 1, but a vanishing integrality witness in a nonzero algebra cannot be that constant; its positive-degree restriction must stay visible.

mathematical_justification: All six contexts use D(f)={p:f∉p}; D(f) is the complement of V((f)) in the prime spectrum. For a prime p, fg∉p iff f∉p and g∉p, so D(fg)=D(f)∩D(g), explaining localized overlap contexts. An idempotent e gives e(1−e)=0, forcing every prime to contain e or 1−e but not both, hence D(e)=V(1−e) is also closed. This special clopen case does not make arbitrary principal opens clopen: D(2) in Spec(Z) excludes the prime (2), and its complement V(2) is not open (every basic neighborhood D(f) of (2), f odd, contains (0)). Existing Spec defines the ambient topological space, not the distinguished subset indexed by f. The associated affine scheme Spec(R_f), sections M_f, an open covering and constructible Boolean combinations are related additional constructions, not identical needed meanings.

mathematical_justification: All five parents use the least ideal containing a specified element a; in their commutative unital rings it is aR={ar:r∈R}. This is an ideal containing a (using 1), and every ideal containing a contains every ar, proving minimality. A generic ideal need not be principal, and a principal ideal need not be prime, maximal or nonzero: (4) in Z is not prime, (0) is principal, and a unit generates the whole ring. The PID meaning universally quantifies principality of every ideal rather than defining the individual construction; finite module generation allows more than one generator and supplies no chosen ideal. For coefficient rings p is the residue characteristic, which may be 0, giving pΛ=0; Cohen-ring p is a positive integer prime. In both cases take its image under Z→Λ, not an assertion that the integer itself is an element without the structure map. The uniformizer is a generator whose ideal equals the maximal ideal, not the ideal object itself.

Formal unramifiedness asks at most one lift; formal étaleness asks exactly one; neither is a property of a bare square-zero ideal. existing_alias_events_examined.reason: Noetherian modules and Noetherian rings both invoke existence of an inclusion-maximal member of every nonempty poset family of respectively submodules or ideals. The abstract maximal-versus-greatest predicate is the same; the eligible family type and Noetherian properties are not identical.

The irreducible-component definition picks an inclusion-maximal irreducible subset among all irreducible subsets of X. The Noetherian ideal/module sources use the same order-theoretic maximal-member predicate in families ordered by inclusion. Irreducibility and Noetherianity are distinct properties.

The connected-component source selects a connected subset C inclusion-maximal among connected subsets of X. That is the ordinary poset definition of maximal element of a specified family of subsets under inclusion: no distinct admissible member properly contains C. The condition that the family consists of connected subsets remains essential and is not promoted to arbitrary maximality; maximal is not greatest or path-connected.

mathematical_justification: All four parents require an admissible member with no strictly larger admissible member in a specified family. This does not mean a greatest member: in the family {{0},{1}} both are maximal and neither contains the other. In the family of ideals {(2),(3)} of Z both are inclusion-maximal, even though a larger ideal (1) exists outside that chosen family. Thus the existing maximal-ideal meaning, which requires properness and maximality among all proper ideals, is not the generic family-relative predicate. Connected and irreducible components restrict admissibility to connected/irreducible subsets; in a discrete two-point space both singleton connected components are maximal, with no greatest connected subset. Noetherian formulations assert existence in EVERY nonempty family, a quantified property stronger than merely defining maximality; an empty family has no member. The subset and poset meanings supply the order but not the generic maximal-member predicate.

mathematical_justification: All four parents require two arrows in the same category with exactly the same source and target; the arrows are not required distinct or equal. Equalizers precompose e into their common source; coequalizers and filteredness postcompose out of their common target. These different directions do not alter the parallel-pair type. Monicity universally tests cancellation on every such pair a,b:W→X; the pair itself is not monicity or an equalizer, and filteredness need not supply a universal coequalizer. Existing category, ordered-pair, limit and colimit meanings package different data or properties rather than this typed diagram prerequisite.

The categorical fibre-product and scheme fibre-product sources each have maps X→S and Y→S and a vertex T or P with maps u:T→X, v:T→Y satisfying fu=gv, i.e. a cone over the cospan-shaped diagram. The generic category-limit source defines a cone on F:I→C by arrows L→F(i) compatible with diagram arrows, with no universality required. Taking I to be the cospan indexing category gives precisely the same underlying cone prerequisite. Pullback universality and the scheme-specific category remain distinct parent conditions; this does not equate arbitrary cones with pullback limits.

mathematical_justification: For each arrow a:i→j in I, a cone has legs λ_i:L→F(i) with F(a)λ_i=λ_j. This is a natural transformation const_L⇒F and contains no universal factorization axiom. Over a single-object identity diagram in Sets, any map L→X is a cone, while a limit leg must be a bijection to X; a singleton mapping into a two-element set separates them. For a cospan X→S←Y, the leg to S is determined by the common composite of the two displayed legs, so fp=gq supplies exactly the specialized cone. Reversing the legs gives a cocone; replacing equality with invertible 2-cells gives pseudocone data, neither the same prerequisite. Existing limit and fibre-product meanings impose universality.

form.52683cac2ccf3bad.locally-ringed-spa.text: A locally ringed space is a topological space X together with a sheaf of rings O_X whose stalk at every point of X is a local ring.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The locally-ringed-space definition uses the stalk O_{X,x} at every point x, which is precisely the sheaf-theoretic filtered colimit of sections on neighborhoods used in the reduced-scheme source's stalk prerequisite. Requiring each stalk to be a local ring remains a condition defining locally ringed spaces, not a property of stalks of every sheaf of rings.

mathematical_justification: A stalk is a germ construction: (U,s) and (V,t) agree iff their restrictions coincide on some neighborhood W⊆U∩V of x. Neighborhoods form a filtered restriction system using intersection. It is not global sections or a categorical fibre. For schemes it gives a local ring, but an arbitrary sheaf of rings need not have local stalks: the constant sheaf Z on a point has stalk Z with multiple maximal ideals. Thus the locally-ringed-space axiom is extra; reducedness of every such local ring is another condition. The set-colimit definition describes underlying germs; ring operations are induced locally, not forgotten.

descriptor.context: Category theory: setoid category

form.74cd6dc48e0606fc.setoid-category.text: A setoid is a groupoid C in which every object has only its identity automorphism; equivalently, between two objects there is at most one arrow, and its existence is an equivalence relation.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: The category-fibred-in-sets formulation and the category-fibred-in-setoids formulation use exactly the same fibre category E_U: objects e of E with p(e)=U and morphisms whose p-image is id_U. Whether the fibre is discrete or a setoid is an additional distinct restriction in the two parent definitions.

mathematical_justification: The strict fibre has objects p(x)=U and only arrows mapped to id_U. It is not generally the full subcategory on those objects: if p is the identity on a nontrivial one-object group category, the full subcategory has all group arrows, but the strict fibre has only the identity. In the groupoid-fibred parents these fibres are groupoids, and discreteness or trivial automorphisms are further restrictions. A setoid can have two distinct isomorphic objects joined uniquely, hence need not be discrete. Fibres at every U being setoids does not imply the whole total category is a setoid; base arrows need not be invertible.

form.wave2.foundation.group.text: A group is a set G with a binary operation *: G×G→G such that (a*b)*c = a*(b*c) for all a,b,c∈G, an element e∈G satisfies e*a = a = a*e for each a∈G, and every a∈G has b∈G with a*b = e = b*a.

form.wave2.foundation.monoid.text: A monoid is a pair (M,⋆) consisting of a set M and an operation ⋆:M×M→M for which (a⋆b)⋆c=a⋆(b⋆c) for all a,b,c∈M and some e∈M satisfies e⋆a=a=a⋆e for every a∈M.

existing_alias_events_examined.reason: Group and monoid sources both require exactly a two-sided identity e for their underlying internal binary operation. Associativity and inverses are distinct conditions of the corresponding object definitions.

mathematical_justification: The common prerequisite is an element e with e*x=x=x*e for every x, without separately requiring associativity or inverses. If e and f are two such elements, e=e*f=f, proving uniqueness. A one-sided identity is insufficient: on a set with x*y=y, every element is a left identity but there is no right identity when at least two elements exist. Both group and monoid parents require two-sided identity; a monoid does not require every element invertible. The historical group→monoid seed is a legitimate consequence, not an identity between arbitrary binary operations and monoids.

mathematical_justification: For a chosen norm and centre a, v↦∥v−a∥ is norm evaluated on an additive difference, not the norm function v↦∥v∥ with centre erased. The triangle inequality implies the induced d(v,a)=∥v−a∥ is a metric; an arbitrary metric need not arise from any vector norm. The two parents evaluate the identical scalar expression then use ≤r versus <r. No completeness, inner product, or equality between closed ball and closure of open ball is required. mathematical_justification: A zero object is one object both initial and terminal. Initial ∅ and terminal singleton in Sets show neither condition alone suffices. Factoring X→0→Y yields a distinguished zero arrow; this works in any pointed category, not only a preadditive one. In a preadditive category a terminal object is also initial: its unique endomorphism is zero and identity, so every arrow out is zero by bilinearity, and each Hom group supplies that arrow. Thus the empty product in the additive-category source supplies a zero object. Object 0, zero morphism, zero composite and exactness are distinct data/conditions.

form.wave2.foundation.orthogonality-meas.text: Let μ be a nonnegative Borel or Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure on a real interval (a,b) and let n be a nonnegative integer such that x↦x^n is μ-integrable. The nth raw moment of μ is μ_n=∫_a^b x^n dμ(x). It is finite only when the integral is finite.

mathematical_justification: With dμ=w(x)1_(a,b)(x)dx, weighted absolute moments become precisely ∫|x|^k dμ. The interval parent separately assumes finite zeroth mass and all positive moments, hence all nonnegative moments as in the measure parent. These are integrability predicates, not the scalar raw moment ∫x^k dμ; for odd k a principal-value cancellation is not Lebesgue absolute integrability. A finite measure can lack a first absolute moment: density x^−2 on [1,∞) has mass 1 and ∫x·x^−2 dx=∞. Each finite polynomial product is bounded by a finite combination of |x|^k, so all absolute moments justify the orthogonality integrals. No density representation is asserted for every Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure.

Pairwise-disjointness and closure under that union are separate source-specific conditions.

mathematical_justification: Countable union of A_n consists of elements belonging to at least one n≥1; repeating or empty terms changes no result. It is the countable-index specialization of arbitrary union, not a disjoint tagged coproduct. Pairwise disjointness adds a condition on inputs, not a different operation. In the alternative sigma axioms, finite unions follow from complements and differences; disjointify A_n as B_n=A_n\(A_1∪…∪A_{n−1}), giving pairwise disjoint B_n with the same union. Thus the restricted closure axiom implies general countable-union closure without changing the candidate operation. Arbitrary-union closure is stronger: countable/cocountable sets on an uncountable X form a sigma-algebra but need not contain an arbitrary union of singletons.

form.26b6764e3ef7a953.pushout.text: Given morphisms B to A and B to C in a category, a pushout is an object P equipped with morphisms A to P and C to P agreeing on B, such that every other compatible pair of maps to an object T factors uniquely through P.

mathematical_justification: For a span B→A,B→C, a compatible pair i:A→P,j:C→P satisfies i f=j g. This is the span-shaped cocone, whose B-component is forced by that equality. It is an instance of a generic cocone but retains a specific input diagram and pair of arrows, not an arbitrary diagram shape, and is not automatically a pushout. In Sets with B=∅ and A=C={*}, two maps to a singleton form such a pair while the pushout is a two-element set; universality fails for that chosen vertex. Do not reverse it into a cone over a cospan or infer that the structure arrows are injective in every category.

form.wave2.foundation.left-module-nonuni.text: Let R be an associative ring and (M,+) an abelian group. A left R-module structure on M is an action R×M→M, (r,m)↦rm, satisfying r(m+n)=rm+rn, (r+s)m=rm+sm, and (rs)m=r(sm). form.wave2.module94.unital-left-module.text: Let R be a ring with identity 1 and let (M,+) be an abelian group. A unital left R-module is an action R×M→M satisfying r(m+n)=rm+rn, (r+s)m=rm+sm, (rs)m=r(sm), and 1m=m for all r,s∈R and m,n∈M.

mathematical_justification: The zero R-module is the singleton additive group with its forced zero action. The final quotient in a regular sequence must not be this object; otherwise injectivity on zero successive terms would make trivial sequences misleading. form.wave2.graph42.simple-undirected.text: A simple undirected graph is a pair G=(V,E), where V is a set of vertices and E⊆{e⊆V:|e|=2}. Thus each edge {u,v} has distinct vertices u≠v, has no direction, and occurs at most once.

mathematical_justification: A circuit here is a positive-length finite closed TRAIL, no undirected edge repeated, whereas a simple cycle forbids repeated vertices except its closing one. Traversing two triangles sharing one vertex in succession is a circuit with that shared vertex repeated, not a simple cycle. Every finite closed trail contains a simple cycle: take a shortest closed subwalk between repeated vertices, whose interior vertices cannot repeat. Thus absence of circuits and cycles agrees in simple undirected graphs even when the ambient vertex set is infinite. This is equality of existence/absence predicates, not identity of the individual circuit and cycle objects, nor a rooted-tree or directed/matroid convention.

form.wave2.real50.cut-model-reals.text: In the Dedekind-cut construction, the underlying set R_D consists of all lower Dedekind cuts A of Q. Define the order by A≤B if and only if A⊆B. form.wave2.real50.dedekind-rational-lowe.text: A (lower) Dedekind cut of the rational numbers is a subset A of Q such that A is nonempty, A is not all of Q, if a belongs to A then every rational q<a also belongs to A, and A has no largest element.

mathematical_justification: The carrier R_D is a subset of P(Q), consisting of all NONEMPTY PROPER downward closed subsets without greatest rational. It is not a single cut, a pair (cut,complement), Q itself, or already a field with operations. Separation from P(Q) is strict: ∅ and Q are subsets but not cuts. The rational example A_q={r:r<q} is nonempty/proper and has no greatest member by rational density. Abstract complete ordered fields are isomorphic to an eventual cut field but not literally the same sets. The source explicitly treats arithmetic and completeness as proof obligations; merely collecting cuts supplies none of them.

form.wave2.foundation.unit-of-ring.text: Let R be an associative ring with identity 1_R. An element u in R is a unit if there exists v in R such that uv=1_R=vu. The identity is required, but u itself need not equal 1_R.

mathematical_justification: For an associative operation with identity e, b is a two-sided inverse of a when ab=e=ba. If b and c are both inverses, b=b(ac)=(ba)c=c. A one-sided inverse need not be two-sided: on N, shift s(n)=n+1 and p(0)=0,p(n+1)=n satisfy p∘s=id but s∘p≠id. The group parent requires such inverse for EVERY a, stronger than a monoid having one invertible element. An inverse element is not an inverse function of a set map; a ring unit is the analogous multiplication predicate in a richer ambient ring and does not force all ring elements invertible.

form.788671763be693df.free-module-resolu.text: A free resolution of an R-module M is an exact augmented chain complex ⋯→F_2→F_1→F_0→M→0 with every F_i a free R-module.

mathematical_justification: For cochains d^i:C^i→C^(i+1), H^i=ker d^i/im d^(i−1) is defined because d^i d^(i−1)=0. A Hom applied to a homological resolution reverses arrows: δ^i(f)=f∘d_(i+1); δ^(i+1)δ^i=0. For the unaugmented F_•, H^0 Hom(F_•,N) identifies Hom(M,N) via augmentation, rather than including Hom(M,N) as a preceding term that would change the computation. Chain homology has opposite degree direction and is not literally cohomology with indices erased. There is an additional existing-edge scope question: the stored internal-Hom MODULE target requires commutative R, while this parent says only R-modules. Over arbitrary associative R, Hom_R is naturally an abelian group; output scalar multiplication need not preserve R-linearity (for M=N=R and noncentral r, r·id fails). form.wave2.bridge136.convex-real.1.text: Let V be a vector space over ℝ and C⊆V. The subset C is convex if for every x,y∈C and t∈[0,1], the vector tx+(1−t)y belongs to C.

form.wave2.bridge136.convex-real.2.context: Real-vector-space convex subset with equivalent two-point and Minkowski-set conditions
form.wave2.bridge136.convex-real.2.display_term: convex subset of a real vector space
form.wave2.bridge136.convex-real.2.text: For a real vector space V and C⊆V, C is convex if tC+(1−t)C⊆C for every t∈[0,1], where tC+(1−t)C={tx+(1−t)y:x,y∈C}.

mathematical_justification: tC+(1−t)C is a SET of all tx+(1−t)y with independent x,y∈C. It is not one pointwise convex combination or merely scalar multiplication of C. For C={0,2}⊆R and t=1/2, this set is {0,1,2}, larger than C; allowing only x=y would falsely yield C for every subset. At t=0 or 1 it equals C for nonempty C, and for C=∅ it is ∅ because there are no input pairs (the image 0∅ is also ∅, not {0}). Inclusion for every t∈[0,1] exactly matches the two-point convexity predicate, with no norm, dimension, closedness or arbitrary-real-scalar stability.

In contrast, merely preserving automorphisms does not put them in the kernel; for F=id the kernel is trivial, while for the map of a group category to terminal every automorphism is killed. The kernel group at x is not the entire relative-inertia category of pairs and intertwining arrows.

form.wave2.foundation.mapping-element-as.text: Given sets X and Y, a mapping f:X→Y assigns to every x∈X exactly one value f(x)∈Y. Equivalently, for each x∈X there exists a unique y∈Y that the assignment associates with x.

mathematical_justification: Restricting f:X→M to U⊆X keeps each value f(u) and changes its domain to U; it is f composed with inclusion U→X. It is neither inverse image of a subset, a sheaf-restriction map as extra sheaf data, nor a new choice of values. Restrictions to the same U preserve pairwise metric errors; uniform convergence there means one N for every y∈U, possibly depending on ε and the chosen neighborhood, not on y. For f_n(x)=x/n on R, every bounded neighborhood has uniform convergence to zero but the whole line does not. form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.text: Let f:[a,b]→R be bounded with a<b. For a finite partition a=x_0<⋯<x_n=b and arbitrary tags ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], let S=Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(x_i−x_{i−1}) and mesh=max_i(x_i−x_{i−1}). The function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with integral L∈R if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |S−L|<ε for every tagged partition with mesh<δ.

mathematical_justification: Boundedness is one M≥0 working for every x in the fixed interval. Pointwise finite values or compactness of the domain alone do not imply it: define f(a)=0 and f(x)=1/(x−a) for x>a. Conversely the Dirichlet indicator of rational inputs is bounded by 1 but not Riemann integrable on a nondegenerate interval: arbitrary tags allow all-rational and all-irrational sums of b−a and 0. Thus boundedness is not integrability, continuity, or bounded-linearity of an operator. A bounded-above range alone is weaker than a two-sided absolute bound; f(x)=−1/(x−a) with f(a)=0 is bounded above but not bounded.

form.03b55b8ca41abb20.jacobson-ring.text: A commutative ring R is a Jacobson ring when every radical ideal I of R equals the intersection of the maximal ideals of R containing I.

form.90b0d1ecfa394230.jacobson-radical-r.text: For a commutative ring R, its Jacobson radical Jac(R) is the intersection of all maximal ideals of R.

form.90b0d1ecfa394230.jacobson-radical-u.text: Equivalently, an element x∈R belongs to Jac(R) exactly when 1−xy is invertible in R for every y∈R.

mathematical_justification: A radical ideal satisfies x^n∈I⇒x∈I for every positive n, equivalently sqrt(I)=I. The radical OPERATION takes any ideal to a new ideal, whereas this is a property of an ideal already given. For example (4) in Z is not radical since 2²∈(4) but 2∉(4), and sqrt((4))=(2). The Jacobson radical is the intersection of maximal ideals of a ring; a Jacobson R requires a relation between all radical ideals and containing maximal ideals, not equality of the predicate radical with that distinguished ideal. In k[t]_(t), (0) is radical and Jac(R)=(t), separating them. I=R is allowed as a radical ideal unless properness is separately imposed; empty intersection then gives R.

form.wave2.foundation.orthogonality-meas.text: Let μ be a nonnegative Borel or Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure on a real interval (a,b) and let n be a nonnegative integer such that x↦x^n is μ-integrable. The nth raw moment of μ is μ_n=∫_a^b x^n dμ(x). It is finite only when the integral is finite.

mathematical_justification: The discrete all-moment condition is Σ_(x∈X)|x|^k w_x<∞ for every k≥0, so k=0 includes total weight finiteness. With atomic measure μ=Σ w_xδ_x it equals all absolute μ-moments, but the stored discrete prerequisite retains support and weights whereas general Stieltjes measures need not be atomic. Positive summability alone does not imply higher moments: X={1,2,…},w_n=1/n² has finite total mass and infinite first moment. Conversely n^k2^−n sums finitely for each fixed k, showing a valid infinite-support example. Different k may have different finite bounds; no single bound uniformly over all k is required.

form.9f75052b1742ab3f.cofiltered-categor.text: A category I is cofiltered if its opposite category I^op is filtered; equivalently I is nonempty, any two objects receive arrows from a common object, and any parallel arrows become equal after precomposition from another object.

mathematical_justification: A pro-object is a formal cofiltered inverse diagram, with its formal morphism structure, not an actual limit object in C or a single inverse-sequence arrow. Ind-objects reverse the formal direction; saying Pro(C) is related to Ind(C^op)^op does not identify objects of the two completions of C without opposites. Essential constancy adds a condition making the formal object isomorphic to a constant one; a cone alone does not establish it.

Generic function restriction keeps the codomain G, whereas this construction includes closure and codomain corestriction; do not erase that distinction.

form.wave2.foundation.field-commutative-.text: A field is a commutative ring k with identity 1_k, with 0≠1_k, such that for every a∈k with a≠0 there exists b∈k satisfying ab=1_k (and hence ba=1_k).

form.wave2.cross107.topological-closure..text: For a subset A of a topological space X, its closure cl_X(A) is the smallest closed subset of X containing A (equivalently, the unique least element under inclusion of the family of closed supersets of A).

mathematical_justification: A closed point means its singleton is closed in the specified ambient space; it does not assert T1 for all points. For x∈Z with Z closed in X, {x} closed in Z is equivalent to closed in X by transitivity of closed subspaces, so there is no conflict between those readings in THIS parent. The generic point of Spec(Z) is not closed, while points (p) are. Jacobson density in every closed Z is extra, not part of being one closed point.

form.5e4b8f6efeda6522.category-fibred-in.text: A functor p:E→C is a category fibred in groupoids if every morphism f:V→U in C lifts to a morphism y→x above f for each object x over U, and each compatible base morphism between the sources of two arrows into x lifts uniquely to a morphism between their domains.

form.e606496d592fe305.relatively-prime-p.text: Polynomials f,g∈k[x] over a field k are relatively prime when the ideal (f,g) they generate is the entire polynomial ring k[x].
Two polynomials f,g over a field k are relatively prime if and only if they have no common zero in an algebraic closure of k.

mathematical_justification: A common zero is one α in a specified extension satisfying BOTH evaluations, not a root of either polynomial independently or a formal gcd. Testing only k-rational zeros is inadequate: over Q, f=g=T²+1 have no rational zero but share roots over an algebraic closure and are not coprime. If gcd=1, a Bezout identity evaluated at a common zero contradicts 1=0; conversely a nonconstant gcd has a root in the algebraic closure. Zero/constant polynomials must retain the same evaluation convention.

form.wave2.foundation13.exact-sequence-a.text: A sequence of arrows in an additive category is a complex when each consecutive composite is zero. When the category is abelian, a complex X→Y→Z is exact at Y if im(X→Y)=ker(Y→Z) as subobjects of Y. An exact complex is exact at every applicable position; a short exact sequence has form 0→A→B→C→0.

form.wave2.foundation13.preadditive-cate.text: For a morphism f:X→Y in a preadditive category, a cokernel is a morphism p:Y→C satisfying p∘f=0, such that for every q:Y→Z with q∘f=0 there is exactly one h:C→Z with q=h∘p. A cokernel is asserted only when such a universal morphism exists.

descriptor.context: Universal-property kernel of a morphism in a preadditive category, existence conditional

form.wave2.foundation13.preadditive-cate.context: Universal-property kernel of a morphism in a preadditive category, existence conditional
form.wave2.foundation13.preadditive-cate.text: For a morphism f:X→Y in a preadditive category, a kernel is a morphism i:K→X satisfying f∘i=0, such that for every j:Z→X with f∘j=0 there is exactly one h:Z→K with j=i∘h. A kernel is asserted only when such a universal morphism exists.

mathematical_justification: In an abelian category Im(f)=ker(coker f) is a subobject of Y, meaning its monomorphism up to isomorphism over Y. This is not a bare underlying-set image in an arbitrary category or the domain X. In groups/modules the usual image yields a concrete representative, but abstractly no element model is assumed. The equation Im(f)=ker(g) imposes exactness on a complex; image existence alone does not imply it. Additivity without the abelian hypotheses does not guarantee all relevant kernels/cokernels exist.

form.7ca4fb934b2f076c.kahler-differentia.text: For a ring map R→S, the module of Kähler differentials Ω_{S/R} is an S-module with a universal R-derivation d:S→Ω_{S/R} such that composition with d gives a bijection Hom_S(Ω_{S/R},M)≅Der_R(S,M) for every S-module M.

form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.context: Classical real analysis: universal sufficiently fine tagged partition integral
form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.display_term: proper Riemann integral on a compact interval
form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.text: Let f:[a,b]→R be bounded with a<b. For a finite partition a=x_0<⋯<x_n=b and arbitrary tags ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], let S=Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(x_i−x_{i−1}) and mesh=max_i(x_i−x_{i−1}). The function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with integral L∈R if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |S−L|<ε for every tagged partition with mesh<δ.

mathematical_justification: A tagged partition consists of both a strictly increasing finite endpoint list and one ξ_i in each closed subinterval. A fixed partition has many tags and endpoint tags are permitted. The scalar sum depends on those choices, while mesh ignores tags. Universal quantification over ALL sufficiently fine tagged partitions cannot be replaced by one fixed sampling rule: rational versus irrational tags separate the Dirichlet indicator sums. The domain is a<b and finite, so no improper-integration or arbitrary infinite-partition convention is added.

form.42730c7ef758df2a.two-fibre-product.text: For 1-morphisms X→Z←Y in a (2,1)-category, a 2-fibre product X×_Z Y is a terminal object, in the 2-categorical sense, among objects W equipped with maps W→X and W→Y and an invertible 2-morphism between the two resulting maps W→Z.

form.42730c7ef758df2a.two-final-object.text: A final object T of a (2,1)-category C is an object such that, for every Y in C, there is a 1-morphism Y→T and any two such 1-morphisms are connected by exactly one 2-morphism.

mathematical_justification: A pseudocone includes two 1-cells and a specified invertible 2-cell between their composites; ordinary cones require equality of composites and contain no such choice. In a 2-category, even equal composite 1-cells can admit different automorphism 2-cells, so forgetting the comparison loses data. The 2-fibre product is universal among these pseudocones, not any one pseudocone. Its terminality is up to the stipulated unique comparison 2-arrows, not ordinary equality of mediating 1-cells.

mathematical_justification: In characteristic prime p, (a+b)^p=a^p+b^p since intermediate binomial coefficients vanish, and (ab)^p=a^pb^p, so Frobenius is a unital endomorphism. It is not an arbitrary field automorphism or the assertion that every element is a pth power. No analogous p=0 map is imposed in characteristic zero.

form.wave2.real50.dedekind-rational-lowe.text: A (lower) Dedekind cut of the rational numbers is a subset A of Q such that A is nonempty, A is not all of Q, if a belongs to A then every rational q<a also belongs to A, and A has no largest element.

mathematical_justification: For a subset of a TOTAL order, having no greatest element is equivalent to every a admitting a strictly larger b. The canonical context states this equivalence while contrasting it with no maximal element in partial orders; that contrast is inaccurate at its stated generality: ∀a∃b>a means no maximal element. A two-point antichain has no greatest element yet both elements are maximal. In the actual source Q is totally ordered, so the cut condition itself is sound; preserve that qualification rather than change cut endpoints or nonemptiness.

form.wave2.pop140.independent-pair.text: For measurable A,B in a probability space (Ω,Σ,P), the events A and B are independent if and only if P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). No positive-probability assumption is required for this product-rule definition.

mathematical_justification: Pairwise disjointness is A_i∩A_j=∅ for DISTINCT i,j. Requiring this also for i=j would force all sets empty. It is not pairwise independence: disjoint positive-probability events have intersection probability zero but product positive. A tagged disjoint union forces disjoint tagged images even if original sets overlap; it does not prove this property of the original family. Countability belongs to this sigma-closure application, not the generic property.

mathematical_justification: Element order is the least positive exponent giving identity, or infinite when none exists; it is not the cardinality of the ambient group or merely an exponent that annihilates the element. mathematical_justification: The pentagon equates the two paths from (((W⊗X)⊗Y)⊗Z) to W⊗(X⊗(Y⊗Z)): two associators versus three with the appropriate tensor identities. Naturality of an associator alone does not imply this: over Q, multiply the usual vector-space associator by 2; it stays natural and invertible, while the paths scale by 4 and 8. Thus pentagon is a real coherence condition, not associativity of a binary set operation or the unit triangle. The full monoidal structure imposes it in addition to its component isomorphisms.

form.wave2.analysis.orthogonal-polynomia.text: Let X⊆R be a countably infinite set of distinct points and assign each x∈X a weight w_x>0 with Σ_{x∈X}|x|^k w_x<∞ for every integer k≥0. A system (p_n)_{n≥0} with deg(p_n)=n is orthogonal on X when Σ_{x∈X}p_n(x)p_m(x)w_x=0 for n≠m.

form.wave2.analysis.orthogonal-polynomia.text: Let X⊆R consist of N+1 distinct points with weights w_x>0. Polynomials p_0,…,p_N, with deg(p_n)=n, form a finite orthogonal polynomial system on X if Σ_{x∈X}p_n(x)p_m(x)w_x=0 for all distinct n,m in {0,…,N}.

mathematical_justification: X has exactly N+1 distinct real points, with N≥0, not an arbitrary sequence with repetitions or countably infinite support. The vector space of real FUNCTIONS on X has dimension N+1. Positive weights make its weighted form positive definite; polynomials of degree≤N inject into these functions since a nonzero such polynomial cannot vanish at all N+1 points. Higher-degree polynomials can vanish on X and have zero weighted norm, so do not infer an infinite nonzero-norm orthogonal system from this finite support. N=0 permits one point.

form.wave2.foundation15.abelian-category.text: An abelian category C is an additive category in which every morphism f has a kernel and a cokernel and, for every such f, the canonical comparison morphism Coim(f)→Im(f) is an isomorphism.

mathematical_justification: Coim(f) is the cokernel of the kernel ARROW into X, with its quotient map from X; it is not ker(f), Im(f) or f itself. For Z --2→ Z the coimage is Z/0, while a concrete image is 2Z. They are canonically isomorphic through the comparison, not literally the same underlying subgroup presentation. Mere additivity/kernel-cokernel availability does not force that comparison to be an isomorphism; the parent imposes the abelian condition.

form.wave2.real50.cut-model-reals.text: In the Dedekind-cut construction, the underlying set R_D consists of all lower Dedekind cuts A of Q. Define the order by A≤B if and only if A⊆B. Each rational q has the canonical representation {r∈Q:r<q}. form.wave2.real50.dedekind-rational-lowe.text: A (lower) Dedekind cut of the rational numbers is a subset A of Q such that A is nonempty, A is not all of Q, if a belongs to A then every rational q<a also belongs to A, and A has no largest element.

mathematical_justification: q↦A_q={r∈Q:r<q} maps into the strict lower-cut carrier: nonempty/properness and absence of a greatest element follow from rational order/density. If q<q′, q belongs to A_(q′) but not A_q, while A_q⊂A_(q′), proving strict order preservation and injectivity. It is not an identity of rational numbers with subsets, an arbitrary field embedding or the constant-Cauchy-class embedding. Preserving field operations requires the separately defined cut arithmetic; no complete ordered-field proof follows from this map alone.

form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.display_term: proper Riemann integral on a compact interval
form.wave2.foundation.tagged-riemann-int.text: Let f:[a,b]→R be bounded with a<b. For a finite partition a=x_0<⋯<x_n=b and arbitrary tags ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], let S=Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(x_i−x_{i−1}) and mesh=max_i(x_i−x_{i−1}). The function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] with integral L∈R if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that |S−L|<ε for every tagged partition with mesh<δ.

mathematical_justification: A finite ordered endpoint list includes a,b and strict intermediate inequalities, so a<b implies at least one positive-width interval. The partition does not choose sample tags or a function f. Closed adjacent subintervals meet at their shared endpoint, so this is not literally the pairwise-disjoint subset partition of candidate228. Equal spacing is optional, not required. The mesh and Riemann sum are derived from the endpoint/tag data and carry additional scalar/function inputs. Infinite partitions and a=b are outside this parent’s stated scope.

form.d8201788fcb507c5.compatible-localiz.text: For elements f_1,…,f_n∈R generating the unit ideal and an R-module M, a compatible family of local sections is a tuple (m_i∈M_{f_i}) whose images agree in M_{f_i f_j} for every pair i,j; such tuples are exactly the image of M under its diagonal localization map.

mathematical_justification: Since D(f_if_j)⊆D(f_i), the restriction goes M_(f_i)→M_(f_if_j), opposite to inclusion of open sets. Concretely m/f_i^n maps to mf_j^n/(f_if_j)^n; this uses commutative localization and is compatible with further restrictions. It need not be injective: for M=Z/2,f_i=1,f_j=2, the target is zero and the nonzero source is killed. Module localization OBJECT, induced restriction arrow and overlap compatibility of a tuple are different data. This is not ordinary domain restriction of a set function.

form.wave2.bridge136.numeric-delta.1.text: For any set Γ, the numerical Kronecker delta is δ:Γ×Γ→{0,1} defined by δ(a,b)=1 when a=b and δ(a,b)=0 when a≠b.

form.wave2.bridge136.numeric-delta.2.text: For a,b∈Γ, the numerical Kronecker delta satisfies δ(a,b)=[a=b], where the Iverson indicator is 1 if the statement a=b is true and 0 otherwise.

mathematical_justification: The Iverson bracket assigns numeric 1 or 0 to an arbitrary proposition P.
